title: Dogma
author: Dn Yonnas
summary: An introduction to the three foundations by which the faith of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is guarded and handed on: Dogma, Canon, and Tradition. Dogma is the unchangeable foundation of belief, Canon is the divinely guided order and discipline of the Church, and Tradition is the living transmission of faith from the fathers to their children.

sections.p: The faith of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church rests upon three things: Dogma, Canon, and Tradition. These are the foundations on which the faith is preserved, established, revealed, known, and handed down. By them we know what we believe and how we are to live, so that the one who understands all three well truly knows his faith and understands how he ought to live.

sections.quote: Remember those who rule over you, who have spoken the word of God to you ... Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever. Do not be carried about with various and strange doctrines.

sections.p: The teacher places the whole lesson under this exhortation: to hold fast to those who handed on the word of God, to imitate the faith of the fathers, and not to be carried away by strange and foreign teachings, because Christ Himself does not change. Dogma, Canon, and Tradition are precisely the appointed paths by which that unchanging faith is kept and carried across the generations.

Dogma means the foundation of faith. It is that which does not change, does not grow old, is not abolished, and is not altered. It is our unchanging belief and teaching concerning God. To abolish or to diminish dogma is denial and error. The word derives from the Greek 'dokeo,' meaning to think, to conceive, or to judge, and so it comes to mean a truth that stands fixed, holding a principle that cannot be abolished or changed. The English dictionaries, the teacher notes, render it as an accepted principle or teaching, a settled position, or a decree laid down by a body within the Church; dogma is therefore a decree that leads the faithful to salvation and to God.
Because they are received as dogma, the central mysteries and doctrines of the Church can neither be improved upon nor changed, for the foundation of the Church's dogma is the unchanging word of God.

list: The Mystery of the Holy Trinity (ምሥጢረ ሥላሴ)
The Mystery of the Incarnation (ምሥጢረ ሥጋዌ)
The Mystery of Baptism (ምሥጢረ ጥምቀት)
The Mystery of the Eucharist (ምሥጢረ ቁርባን)
The Mystery of the Resurrection of the Dead (ምሥጢረ ትንሣኤ ሙታን)
The doctrine concerning Mary (ነገረ ማርያም) and the doctrine concerning the Saints (ነገረ ቅዱሳን)
The Five Pillars of Mystery and the Holy Scriptures, which are likewise counted as dogma

sections.p: All of these are regarded as dogma, and therefore they are not revised and not changed. Within the Tewahedo confession this means holding firmly that God is one essence in three Persons; that the Word became truly incarnate, being one incarnate nature of God the Word; and that the saving mysteries of Baptism, the Eucharist, and the Resurrection are received as God has given them, never to be diminished by human invention.

sections.h2: Canon (Kanona) — The Order and Discipline of the Church

sections.p: Canon, the teacher explains, comes from the Greek 'kanon,' meaning a measure or measuring rod, and so law, order, rule, and judgment. It points to the order that exists within the Church. In Geez it derives from the verb 'qanana,' meaning to legislate, to make, to establish a rule, to give a canon. God Himself gave us such order, saying, 'This shall be an everlasting statute for you,' and Scripture commands that all things be done decently and in order.

sections.quote: Let all things be done decently and in order.

sections.p: Canons are decisions built upon the teaching of the Holy Scriptures, established by the holy Apostles and by the fathers and bishops who followed them. Because these decisions were made under the guidance of the Holy Spirit, the Church honors them as the word of God. Many were also formed in response to disputes and controversies that arose in various ages, becoming the canon of the Church. Saint Paul, having taught how the order of the Eucharist is to be carried out, said that he would set the rest in order when he came; and the councils that fixed the number of the canonical Scriptures had a similar purpose.

We must distinguish law, command, and order. Where a law says 'do not,' and a command says 'do,' order (sirat) is the pure and upright decision that is born from law and carried out by command; it gathers together both law and commandment. God Himself is the teacher of order, that order is a medicine, and that by keeping order we express our submission to God. God first wrought order through Moses, and afterward established firm order through the Apostles; later the Three Hundred and Eighteen fathers, drawing from the Scriptures, made for us laws, rules, and order. What the Apostles and the councils of their successors established no one may alter, since these things are drawn from the books God Himself caused to be written.

Among the things appointed by canon and order are the seasons of fasting, the days of feasts, the number and naming of the canonical Scriptures, the order of prayer, the removing of shoes to enter the sanctuary, praying turned toward the east, the preparations required before receiving the Holy Eucharist, and the lamps that are lit during the Divine Liturgy. Unlike dogma, such canonical order may, where it serves the good of the Church, be amended by the decision of the Holy Synod.

The first canon of the Church was set by the Apostles themselves. In the days of the Apostles, some who came to Christianity from Judaism troubled the Church, insisting that Gentile believers could not be saved unless they were circumcised according to the law of Moses, filling the Church with strife and dispute. To resolve this the Apostles first gathered the council at Jerusalem, and after deliberating they decreed a canon, laying upon the believers no greater burden than the necessary things.

sections.quote: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things.

sections.h3: The Sources of the Church's Canon

sections.p: Although the canon of the Church today has many sources, including the Holy Scriptures, the teacher names four that are cited in a special way as sources of the canon.

list: The Synod of the Apostles — most of the canons are gathered in the two holy books called the Canons of the Apostles, namely the Sinodos and the Didascalia.
The Ecumenical Councils — at which the fathers, besides condemning heretics, established canons; these are the Council of Nicaea, the Council of Constantinople, and the Council of Ephesus.
The National (Local) Councils — synods held in various lands and regions, among them the councils of Ancyra, Carthage, Gangra, Antioch, Laodicea, and Sardica.
The Decisions of the Fathers — canons laid down by individual fathers, such as the canons of Hippolytus of Rome, of Basil, of Gregory of Nyssa, and of John Chrysostom.

The Council of Nicaea (325): among its canons it was decreed that the feast of the Resurrection be kept only on Sunday, and that in a diocese only the bishop of that diocese may confer ordination; twenty canons were laid down.

The Council of Constantinople (381): the fathers confirmed that the decision of the Nicene fathers must not be opposed by anyone, and decreed that those returning from heresy to the Orthodox faith be received once they confessed the straight faith; seven canons were laid down.
The Council of Ephesus (431): it was decided that the Church of Cyprus should be self-governing (autocephalous); eight canons were laid down.
By it heretics and heresy are detected and set apart.
It causes the service of the Church to be carried out in good order.
It guards the unity of the Church (Acts 15:1-29).
It serves to distinguish what belongs to the Church from what does not.

sections.h2: Tradition (Tewfit) — The Handing On of the Faith

sections.p: Tradition (tewfit) means transmission or handing on. It points to the religious heritage passed from the fathers to the children: the teaching, next after the word of Scripture, which tells us of Christianity and which we have received from the holy Apostles and from our fathers. These are things not written in the Bible, yet which in no way depart from the teaching of the Bible; they are the spiritual practices our fathers received from God and which were pleasing to God. Those who reject this have also lost what the Church received from the fathers to whom God bore witness, namely the history and teaching of the Apostles and the decisions of the ancient synods.

The Geez root 'awfeye' means to give, to entrust, to hand over, to commit as a charge. Tradition is thus the upright faith of the Apostles handed down word for word from the ancient fathers, together with the writings we received from the holy Apostles. The teacher likens it to a pure drink that flows from a good spring, undiluted and unspoiled by the passing of the ages.

sections.h3: Tradition Before the Scriptures Were Written

sections.p: Tradition is the path by which the faith was handed on even before the Bible was written. Abel offered the firstborn of his flock and their fat, and our fathers Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob offered the sacrifices that pleased God, not because they had learned them in writing, but because they had seen them from their fathers. The Scriptures themselves command us to receive tradition, and commend those who hold it fast, while also commanding us to separate from those who walk apart from it.

sections.quote: Therefore, brethren, stand fast and hold the traditions which you were taught, whether by word or our epistle.

sections.h3: Tradition in the Age of the Apostles

sections.p: The holy Apostles taught their followers the Christian teaching they had learned from our Lord Jesus Christ by tradition: they preached the Gospel by word, by deed, and by their lives. The children of the Church received what they saw, heard, and learned from the Apostles and their disciples, and by living it they handed it on to the next generation. The Apostles even made use of the holy tradition of the Jews. So Matthew records the prophecy 'He shall be called a Nazarene,' which is not found in the forty-six books of the Old Testament; the Church holds that it was spoken by the prophets in books lost during the captivity, yet preserved by word until it reached the Apostles.
The teacher gathers further examples in which the apostolic writers preserve what was handed down rather than written in the earlier Scriptures.

list: Hebrews 12:21 records that Moses said, 'I am exceedingly afraid and trembling,' which is not written in the law (Exodus 19:16-25); Paul recorded what he received from tradition.
2 Timothy 3:8 names Jannes and Jambres as those who withstood Moses; Exodus 7:11 speaks only of 'the magicians of Egypt' without their names, but Paul gives their names from tradition.
Acts 20:35 preserves the Lord's saying, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive,' which is not recorded in the Gospels but reached us through tradition.

Jude 1:9 recounts the dispute of the archangel Michael with the devil over the body of Moses; the end of Deuteronomy says only that Moses died on Mount Nebo and that his grave is unknown, and Jude drew this account from the traditional book, the Assumption of Moses.

sections.p: Thus the ancient and apostolic Church received teachings, testimonies, and orders handed down from the Lord and from the Apostles that are not recorded in the Gospel, as Scripture itself testifies (2 Thessalonians 2:15; 1 Corinthians 11:34; Titus 1:5; 2 John 12; 3 John 13-14; John 20:30).

list: Material traditions — those that are handled and held, which have been passed to us, such as vestments, the prayer staff (meqomiya), and the like.
Written (book) traditions — the teachings written in books and handed down to us.

Practical traditions — the spiritual practices we perform after seeing our fathers and mothers do them, such as the manner of dress, the orders of the cup-fellowships (mahbers), the way of approaching and venerating the church, and the order of making the sign of the cross.

sections.p: The Church does not accept just any tradition as Christian. There are clear standards by which a tradition is verified to be a true Christian tradition.

list: The word of God (Scripture).
The Didascalia.
The decisions of the Ecumenical Councils.
The sayings of the fathers (bihilata abew).

sections.p: As the teacher concludes, dogma is that by which we know what we believe about God and how our faith differs from others, and by which we are guarded from error; canon is the order we keep and the life we live as Christians and members of the one Church when we gather together as a community; and tradition is the good life, pure worship, and upright teaching we have inherited from our fathers. Held together under the unchanging word of God, these three guard the faith and hand it on, faithful to the apostolic confession of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.
